summary: A description of the Telnet logger and server for the CP/CMS system on the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67, listed as host 10. It serves half and full duplex users with ASCII or EBCDIC data, uses the hide-input and no-echo controls during login, and follows the initial connection protocol. The text says it was not cleared for public release.

eli5.summary: A guide to how one particular computer lets people sign in remotely by typing, including how it handles passwords being hidden.

subtitle: A Telnet implementation for the Lincoln Lab CP/CMS system on the ARPANET

tldr.problem: The CP/CMS system at Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 operated with EBCDIC character codes but needed to work with ARPANET Telnet clients using ASCII; it also needed to handle both half-duplex and full-duplex terminals.
tldr.mechanism: The Telnet logger and server translated between ASCII and EBCDIC, negotiated character codes at login, managed line buffering for the half-duplex CP/CMS system, and mapped Telnet control codes to CP/CMS controls for features like password hiding and interrupt handling.
tldr.outcome: The LL-67 system could serve multiple simultaneous Telnet users with transparent character code conversion, enabling network users to log in and access CP/CMS despite the fundamental differences in character encoding.

today: RFC 466 is a historical technical document describing one of the earliest Telnet server implementations. EBCDIC has largely been superseded by UTF-8 and ASCII in modern systems, but the translation and control flow concepts remain relevant.

sections.title: The Lincoln Laboratory TELNET System
sections.content: J. Winett documented the Telnet logger and server for CP/CMS running on the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 computer (host 10). The document was marked as not cleared for public release and intended only for ARPA network use. The facility served both half-duplex and full-duplex Telnet users, and supported data in either ASCII or EBCDIC character codes. It used Telnet hide-your-input and no-echo controls during login for password security, and sent Telnet control breaks as input prompts for half-duplex terminals.
sections.eli5: Lincoln Lab's computer needed a system to let people sign in from the network. It handled two kinds of terminals and two kinds of character codes.

sections.title: Login and Authentication
sections.content: When a user initiated a Telnet connection using the ICP protocol, the logger would ask whether to operate in ASCII or EBCDIC by waiting for a data type code or null line. It then displayed the welcome message in the appropriate code. The login procedure expected the user to enter LOGIN userid, after which CP would ask for a password. A special LOGGER FILE mapped network userids and passwords to CP system credentials, adding a security boundary between the network and the CP system. Invalid credentials were passed to CP, which would reject them, and the response sent back to the network user.
sections.eli5: The logger asked what code the user's terminal used, then checked if the network user's password was in a special file before letting CP process the login.

sections.title: ASCII and EBCDIC Translation
sections.content: Since CP/CMS operated with EBCDIC, incoming ASCII had to be translated to EBCDIC before being sent to virtual machines. The server included detailed ASCII-to-EBCDIC mapping tables for all 128 ASCII characters plus Telnet control codes. The CR-LF (carriage return-line feed) sequence from ASCII was mapped to EBCDIC NL (newline). Telnet control codes like NOP, hide-your-input, and break were mapped to their EBCDIC equivalents or equivalent functions. Output worked similarly, with EBCDIC codes mapped back to ASCII or mapped to Telnet control codes as appropriate.
sections.eli5: The system had a table to convert each ASCII letter and symbol to the matching EBCDIC code, so the computer could understand what the user typed.

sections.title: Half-Duplex and Line Buffering
sections.content: CP/CMS expected input line-by-line with characters buffered until a newline was received. The half-duplex nature meant characters were only examined when the system expected input. Telnet control breaks were sent as end-of-message markers and input prompts. A full-duplex user Telnet could ignore the break prompt, while half-duplex terminals would treat it as a signal that the system was ready for input. A Telnet SYNC was sent when CP needed to abort input to send priority output. No codes in the output stream could cause the Telnet data mark to be transmitted.
sections.eli5: The system waits for a full line of input at a time. It sends a special signal to tell the user's terminal when it is ready for more input.
